description:
Tuwaiq Lunar | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

Tuwaiq Lunar is a Saudi-led, multidisciplinary space engineering team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 through the Universal Event.

Our team is tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by developing an interactive, scientifically grounded platform using NASA data to analyze lunar terrain, solar illumination, Earth visibility, and mission feasibility.

Our members bring expertise in Mechanical Engineering, Aerospace Engineering, Remote Sensing, GIS, and scientific data analysis.

We aim to combine engineering simulations, scientific accuracy, and advanced visualization to help users evaluate and compare potential lunar landing sites.

We are seeking members skilled in Software Engineering, Python, Full-Stack Development, 3D Visualization, and UI/UX Design.

Our mission is to transform complex lunar data into an accessible and reliable decision-support tool.
summary:
Lunar Navigator is a free bilingual (English/Arabic) web app that shows whether a lander at the Moon's south pole will see the Sun for power and Earth for radio, at any hour from 2026 to 2035.

Users pick one of NASA's nine Artemis candidate regions, or click any point, and choose a time. Hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons are compared with the real skyline traced from NASA LOLA laser terrain maps. The app shows Sun and Earth elevation and time to sunset and Earthset, in 3D and in plain words. It also gives landing windows for a full stay, a 10-year calendar, a late-landing test, landing-accuracy ranges, the longest night for battery sizing, distance to permanent shadow (possible ice), LRO CRaTER radiation, and a side-by-side comparison of all regions.

Every part is checked against NASA: JPL positions within 1.4 arcseconds, and sunlight within 0.29 points of NASA's illumination maps. The app also lists what it does not model.

This answers the challenge: compare sites and dates using the Sun and Earth against the local horizon, for planners and the public. At the pole the Sun skims the horizon, so one ridge can mean days of darkness or a lost radio link. Spots a few hundred metres apart differ hugely: at Mons Mouton Plateau, Sun and Earth are up together 19% of the time at the centre but 69% at our pick. Lunar Navigator turns specialist NASA data into a page anyone can open in a browser.
details:
We built Lunar Navigator around one practical question. If a lander touches down at a particular spot near the Moon's south pole, will it get sunlight for power and a clear view of Earth for radio? And for how long?

You pick one of the nine landing regions NASA announced in 2024, click a point on the ground and choose a time between November 2026 and the end of 2035. The site takes hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA JPL Horizons and checks them against the hills and crater rims around that point. We trace the skyline in 720 directions, out to 250 km, using NASA's LOLA terrain maps. Close to the sites NASA has mapped in detail, that terrain is accurate to 5 m.

You don't just get numbers. You can look at the Moon from space, then drop down and stand on your chosen point to watch the Sun and Earth move along its skyline. The site tells you how high each one is, how high the terrain is in that direction and when it will slip behind the hills. Extra map layers show terrain height, sunlight percentage and the permanently shadowed ground where ice could survive.

We wanted people to see how much the exact spot matters. Every region has a centre point and what we call "Our pick". To choose it, we screened the region against NASA's published landing criteria, modelled the 40 strongest candidates in full and kept the best of them. At Mons Mouton Plateau, the Sun and Earth are up together 19.2% of the time at the centre and 68.7% at our pick. That doesn't make our pick a certified landing site or the best point in the whole region. It shows how much conditions can vary inside a single region.

Timing matters just as much. The planner has a calendar, landing windows for the length of stay you choose, a battery estimate and a test for late landings. In one example at Malapert Massif, the Sun and Earth stay up together for a full six-day stay. Land a week late and that drops to 10%, even though both are still up at touchdown. The site also shows how missing the target by up to 100 m would change the result. You can compare all nine regions, change the visibility rules, ask Navi to explain a number and download the hourly data.

The site is written in JavaScript, HTML and CSS. It uses three.js for the 3D views, GSAP for animation and Vite to build it, with Node.js and Python scripts to prepare and check the NASA data. It runs in any browser, on a phone or a computer, in English or Arabic, in light or dark mode.

We checked samples of our results against separate JPL Horizons calculations and NASA's own sunlight maps, and the results of those checks are on the site. We're also clear about what the model can't tell you:

- Seeing Earth doesn't guarantee a working radio link.

- A battery estimate isn't a power system design.

- Permanent shadow doesn't prove there's ice.

- The CRaTER radiation figures aren't a prediction of crew dose.

We wanted people to explore a landing decision for themselves instead of trusting a single map or score. Change the place, the time or the length of the stay, and you can see what changes and why.

LOLA polar illumination and Earth visibility maps (Mazarico et al. 2011)
Landing requirements: NASA Artemis Human Landing System update, 2024
3D Moon texture: NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LROC colour map)
LRO CRaTER dose rates (NASA LRO instrument, data hosted by the University of New Hampshire team)
